claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a typical ferrite-pearlite microstructure.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel is covered by a native, as-formed iron oxide layer.
The onset of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel is governed by the integrity of its native iron oxide film.
At room temperature, the naturally formed oxide film is compact and limits corrosive attack.
Elevated temperature causes thermal stress and increased cation diffusion in the native oxide film.
Thermal stress and increased cation diffusion cause oxide-film spallation, cracking, or localized breakdown.
Loss of oxide-film integrity exposes fresh metal and accelerates corrosion.
Corrosion behavior can be isolated by comparing Q235 samples whose native oxide is preserved with samples whose oxide is chemically removed.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution is an applicable corrosive test environment for a Q235-based specimen.
The governing structural mediator is the continuity, adhesion, and defect density of the native iron oxide film.
An intact native oxide film limits diffusion of corrosive species to the underlying metal.
Enhanced ion mobility and thermal expansion at elevated temperature compromise oxide-film integrity.
Exposure of fresh metal following film breakdown triggers accelerated localized anodic dissolution.
At approximately 25 degrees Celsius, oxide-intact samples will have lower corrosion rates than oxide-removed samples.
At approximately 70 degrees Celsius, initially oxide-intact samples will have significantly higher corrosion rates than at room temperature.
At approximately 70 degrees Celsius, initially oxide-intact samples will have significantly higher corrosion rates than oxide-free samples.
Elevated-temperature exposure will produce more pitting or other localized corrosion morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies in aqueous media without deposition of an additional protective scale and up to approximately 70-80 degrees Celsius.
Extreme temperatures or non-aqueous media may be governed by other corrosion processes.
The precise film-failure temperature and quantitative corrosion-rate increase are not known and require experimental determination.

contradictions.description: The mechanism assigns a protective barrier function to the intact film and says its failure exposes fresh metal, but the elevated-temperature prediction states that initially oxide-intact samples will corrode more than samples whose metal was deliberately exposed by complete oxide removal. No additional mechanism is supplied to explain why breakdown of a formerly protective film should be more damaging than having no film initially.
